Since 1789

The median age of every Congress, from the 1st to the 119th.

Every character in the chamber is one member on opening day, January 3, 2025. Its shape and color are that member's generation. Move over a portrait to light it up.

    Every Congress since 1789

    About this chart

    Each column is one Congress, measured on the day it first convened (January 3 for the 115th to 119th, the Congresses in the chamber, shaded). Voting members only; territorial delegates are left out until statehood. Birth dates are missing for up to a third of members in the earliest Congresses, so those medians use known dates only. In older records a member who filled a vacancy is listed for the whole Congress, so a few seats count two people. Congress grew from 89 to 535 voting members, so counts before 1913 are not directly comparable.

    All members

    How the game works
    What is real
    Every member, age and election. The rosters are everyone seated on January 3 of 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025. Your character, Quorum the pigeon and the dialogue are made up.
    Your age
    Everyone starts at 25 in 2017, the youngest the House allows, so you are old enough for a House seat the whole game. You are 33 by 2025. The Senate requires 30, which you reach in 2022. At each election the game uses your age at the next swearing-in.
    Still there
    After each election the game checks whether the member you picked is still in the same chamber in the new Congress. If they are, you keep walking.
    Seat open
    The member is no longer in that chamber: they retired, lost, died, resigned or moved to the other chamber. The game follows the person, not the district, because district lines were redrawn along the way. It names a successor only when a brand-new member holds the same seat.
    Still waiting
    The member was still there after all four elections, 2018 to 2024.
    75 or older
    The row of characters at the top of the walk has one # for each member 75 or older; the brighter ones were added since 2017. The game counts members who were 75 or older on January 3 of each Congress: 32 in 2017 and 54 in 2025. The seat picker lights them, but you can pick anyone. The Chamber page headline uses 70 or older, so its numbers are larger. The game says nothing about any member's ability; it only counts ages and years in office.
    Who took the seats
    The picture at the end has one small figure for each brand-new member who took a seat that a 2017 member left, 2019 to 2025, grouped by their age on the day they were sworn in: under 35, 35 to 49, 50 or older. Seats with no brand-new member in the same seat afterward are left out. Your group is the one that holds your age when your seat opened, or in 2025 if it never did.
    When they were your age
    After you pick a seat, Quorum names one event from the generation timeline on the Chamber page (Generations): the one closest to the year that member turned 25, your age at the start. The age shown is the age they turned that year. Each event's source is listed under About this site.
    New members
    "New" means not in Congress two years earlier. Their median age is the middle value of their ages on January 3.
    Your choices
    What you do between elections is a made-up example and does not change any ending. The number beside each one is real: how many people in the 2025 Congress list the same thing in their own profiles, from the Congressional Research Service, Membership of the 119th Congress: A Profile (R48535, updated August 4, 2025). The numbers are not added up, because one member can be counted in several.
    Fast forward
    Arithmetic only. First election that could seat you: the first even-year election after which you would be 25 (House) or 30 (Senate) at swearing-in. "You reach the median age": the year you turn the 2025 median age, rounded up. The lit seats are members born before 1992, the year your character was born.
    What it never does
    It never gives odds and never says you would have won. Nobody has measured how much any one step raises a person's chance of reaching Congress, so the game does not make up a number for it.

        About this site

        How to read the chamber, how the numbers were made, and where everything comes from.

        How to read the chamber

        Where each seat sits

        Seats are ordered left to right by voting record, House outside and Senate inside. It is not the real seating plan.

        Character and color are generation

        Each generation has its own character. Its color runs from its oldest members to its youngest.

        xLitxDimEmpty

        Lit and dim

        Lit seats match the view, generation and tool you have open. Dim seats do not. Dashed ovals are empty seats. A seat with a dashed outline is unknown for your filter: not on the source list for a trait, or too few shared votes to compare in the quiz. Unknown is never counted as a no. For race, members on no list are drawn dim, but the count still lists them as unknown.

        Jan 3opening day

        Age on opening day

        Age is measured on January 3 of the first year of each Congress.

        Who's like you?

        What the trait labels mean

        Blank means the sources don't say. It never means "no."

        Details

        Race and ethnicity labels come from Wikipedia lists of members, not from self-identification, and a member who is not listed is unknown, not White. Religion is self-reported and compiled by Pew Research Center. Immigrant background counts come from Pew and are minimums. A blank means the sources do not say. No filter is based on how a portrait looks.

        How would you vote?

        How the issue quiz matches

        8 real votes. Some split by party, so matches partly sort by party.

        Details

        The issue quiz uses 8 roll-call votes from the 119th Congress, picked because they are easy to explain and cover different topics. Four split mostly by party, so matches partly sort by party. That is a property of the votes, not a recommendation. Votes are matched to the same issue in each chamber, which sometimes meant two different but parallel resolutions.

        How the numbers were made

        Who is counted
        Every member seated on January 3 of each Congress, from the 115th (2017) to the 119th (2025). The roster is from unitedstates/congress-legislators.
        Age
        Measured on January 3 of that Congress's first year. The median US age is from Census estimates and exists only for 2020 to 2025.
        Generations
        Birth years follow Pew Research Center.
        Seat order
        Left to right by voting record (Voteview DW-NOMINATE). It is not the real seating plan.
        Unknown is not no
        A missing religion or immigrant value is shown as unknown, never as a no. Race labels come from Wikipedia lists, not from members themselves, and a member on no list is not counted as White. Immigrant counts are minimums.
        Since 1789
        Age is measured on the day each Congress first convened. Voting members only. Birth dates are missing for up to a third of the earliest members, and Congress grew from 89 to 535 members, so early counts are not directly comparable.
        The 8 votes
        Agreement is counted only over votes both you and a member cast. Missed votes are skipped. Matches are never ranked.
        The game
        Members, ages and elections are real. The character, the pigeon and the dialogue are made up. It never gives odds.
        Known gaps
        Six members have no portrait. The chamber, portraits and traits cover 2017 to 2025 only.

            How would you have voted?

            8 real votes. Answer as you go and the chamber keeps whoever voted like you.

            Match
            How matching works

            Four of these votes split mostly by party (overdraft fees, Canada tariffs, Iran, Arctic oil), so matches partly sort by party. The other four drew dozens of members across party lines. Members stay lit when they voted the same way as you on the votes you answered. "All but one" allows one difference once you have 3 votes in common; "all but two" allows two once you have 5. Votes a member missed are skipped, never counted as disagreement; a member who missed too many to compare gets a dashed outline. Matches are not ranked. "What it does" is based on each bill's summary by the Congressional Research Service, Congress's nonpartisan research office.
